title: Finite-state machine
summary: A finite-state machine (FSM) is a mathematical model of computation that can occupy exactly one state from a finite set at any moment. It changes states via transitions triggered by inputs. Two main types exist: deterministic, where one input yields one next state, and non-deterministic, where one input may lead to multiple possible next states (an equivalent deterministic version can always be constructed). FSMs have less computational power than Turing machines due to limited memory defined solely by their state count. Physical devices like vending machines, elevators, traffic lights, and combination locks exhibit FSM behavior. In a turnstile example, states are Locked and Unlocked; a coin input unlocks, and a push input after passing resets to Locked.

mechanisms.title: State transition via inputs
mechanisms.explanation: An FSM resides in one of a finite number of states. A transition to a new state occurs when a specific input is received. The same input may produce different transitions depending on the current state, such as a coin unlocking a turnstile only when it is locked.

mechanisms.title: Deterministic vs. non-deterministic classification
mechanisms.explanation: Deterministic finite-state machines produce exactly one next state per input, while non-deterministic ones may have multiple possible next states for a single input. Any non-deterministic FSM can be converted into an equivalent deterministic FSM, preserving the language it accepts.
